proposal.original_claim_summary: The card combines Forest Service staffing losses, alleged prescribed-burn reductions and suppression policy with the deaths of four federal firefighters in a Colorado burnover, presenting the deaths as a wildfire-policy failure.

identified_problems.explanation: Workforce/policy changes and the June 27, 2026 Knowles Fire burnover are separate events that require independent sourcing.
Three firefighters died at the June 27 burnover; a fourth firefighter died July 24 from injuries, so the card's phrasing that four died on June 27 is incorrect.
The incident was the Knowles Fire burnover; the stored reference to the 'Snyder Fire' is not supported by the official fatality release.
An accident investigation remained underway, so staffing or suppression policy should not be asserted as the cause of the fatalities.
The specific prescribed-burn acreage decline in the card was not verified by the sources examined.

frozen_original.title: Wildfire Policy Failure: Prescribed Burns Halved, Four Firefighters Dead
frozen_original.synopsis: In 2025, the U.S. Forest Service — having lost 16% of its workforce (5,860 staff) under DOGE cuts — reduced hazardous fuel treatment by 1.5 million acres compared to 2024, including cutting prescribed burns nearly in half from over 1.6 million acres to roughly 900,000 acres. Agriculture Secretary Rollins and Interior Secretary Burgum then ordered a sweeping 'full suppression' policy for 2026, abandoning decades of science-backed managed fire strategies. On June 27, 2026, four federal firefighters died when the Snyder Fire in Colorado overran their position. Trump created the U.S. Wildland Fire Service by secretarial order — pulling 3,900 Interior firefighters from six agencies — without congressional approval. By August 2026, millions of acres were burning across the West under unprecedented drought conditions.

claims.notes: The available research record does not establish the claim as written; no corrected narrower claim is emitted.

proposal.exact_defects: The July 2025 timing and claimed catastrophic new backlog are contradicted by Social Security Administration performance releases. On July 7 and July 23, SSA reported that its initial disability backlog had fallen about 25% from 1.2 million to roughly 940,000-950,000 cases, with improved processing and hearing wait times. I did not find support for millions facing newly crippling delays caused by July DOGE cuts.

frozen_original.title: DOJ Under Bondi Opens Criminal Investigation Into Liz Cheney
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, the DOJ under Attorney General Pam Bondi opened a criminal investigation into former Republican Representative Liz Cheney, one of only two House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump for January 6 and who later served as vice chair of the House January 6 committee. The investigation, ostensibly related to the January 6 committee's handling of evidence and witness interviews, was widely condemned as an act of political retaliation against a Republican who had broken with Trump. Cheney publicly stated she would not be intimidated and called the investigation an attempt to silence political opponents through criminal prosecution. The case was seen as a direct warning to any public official who dared hold Trump accountable.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump Cuts Social Security Field Offices by 50%
proposal.original_synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration and DOGE directed the Social Security Administration to close approximately half of its field offices nationwide — roughly 600 of the approximately 1,200 offices that served as the primary in-person contact points for seniors, disabled people, and survivors applying for or managing Social Security benefits. The closures were coupled with mass layoffs of SSA field staff. Seniors and disabled individuals who could not navigate online or phone systems — a substantial portion of the elderly and disabled population — lost their primary access point to benefits they had paid into their entire working lives. Wait times for determinations on disability applications, which had already stretched to over a year, were projected to extend dramatically further. The administration framed the closures as efficiency improvements despite the clear degradation of service.
